steps.title: Soft and spicy
steps.body: Carmenère gives deep purple-red wines with blackberry, plum and red pepper, plus spice, paprika, tobacco and sometimes chocolate. Tannins are soft and acidity moderate, so it feels round and smooth. When not fully ripe, it shows a strong green pepper note.

steps.title: Crimson leaves
steps.body: Its name comes from carmin, the French for crimson, because its leaves turn bright red in autumn before falling. Carmenère is part of the Cabernet family; DNA shows it's a cross of Cabernet Franc and Gros Cabernet. Like its relatives, it has methoxypyrazines, which give green notes when grapes aren't fully ripe.

steps.prompt: Where does Carmenère's name come from?
options: The crimson colour of its autumn leaves
steps.explanation: Carmin means crimson; the leaves turn red in autumn.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Carmenère is deep coloured with a purple rim. On the nose, ripe plum and blackberry with a distinctive spicy, green or red pepper note. On the palate, it's smoother and softer than Cabernet Sauvignon, with less grip. That combination of soft tannin and peppery spice is the clue.

steps.prompt: Carmenère usually has firmer tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Carmenère is softer and rounder, with gentler tannins.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère gives plum, spice and a peppery note
Its name comes from its crimson autumn leaves
It's softer than Cabernet, with a green edge when unripe
